paras: The lynching of Navajo Frank was the hanging of Francisco Tajoya, an Indian prisoner known as Navajo Frank, by a crowd of citizens at Las Vegas, New Mexico, in late June 1882. Accused of lassoing a man named R. H. Hutter and dragging him through the street, he was captured by a posse, then taken from the jail by force and hanged from a telegraph pole. A St. Louis telegraphic special carried the story nationally, often under headlines that cast the hanging as a fitting punishment.

According to the St. Louis special, Hutter was walking in the street with his wife on a Saturday night when a mounted man the dispatch called 'an Indian desperado' threw a lariat around his neck and spurred his horse. Hutter was dragged a hundred yards or more over the rocky street until a bystander fired a revolver at the rider, who cut the lariat near his saddle and fled. Hutter was left 'terribly bruised and mangled', his beard torn out, but was expected to recover.

A mounted posse soon caught the rider, brought him back to town and placed him in jail. In the wire's account, a crowd of citizens gathered at the jail 'between 12 and 1 o'clock' and demanded the prisoner; when this was refused, they forced their way in and the cell keys were handed over. Navajo Frank resisted desperately but was roped, marched to a telegraph pole and hoisted up.

The wire was dated June 27 and said the lynching took place 'yesterday', and the Huntsville Gazette dated it 'On the 26th'. The Ottawa Free Trader likewise placed it 'early on Monday morning', which suggests the hour given in the wire was just after midnight.
No report of an inquest, of any arrest of the lynchers or of an official response appears in the coverage.

The story reached readers mainly through the St. Louis special, printed from June 27 in the Memphis Public Ledger and in papers from Yankton to Canton, Ohio. Some papers ran a short form of the wire under crime-column heads such as 'CRIMINAL', while others printed the full text with Hutter's injuries described in detail. Headlines often made the lynching a matter of deserved punishment: 'A Fiendish Deed' in the Memphis Daily Appeal, 'Brutality Punished' in the St. Paul Daily Globe, and 'A Noose for a Noose' in the Salt Lake Herald.

The Wheeling Daily Intelligencer called it 'The Singular Trick of an Indian Desperado' that 'Judge Lynca Settles', and the Woodsfield Spirit of Democracy credited the hanging to 'Indignant Citizens'. The Marietta Journal ran the same text as late as July 6 under 'A FIEND'S FATE'. The text itself repeatedly called the prisoner 'the fiendish Indian', and none of the papers examined questioned the crowd's action.

The Ottawa Free Trader printed the case under 'Judge Lynch' beside a lynching at Raton the same day and added, without a source, that Navajo Frank had ridden with Billy the Kid's gang and killed twenty men.

Accounts differ on when the lynching occurred. A shorter version of the St. Louis wire said the citizens lynched him 'the same night' as the lassoing, while a separate Las Vegas dispatch dated June 29 told the Los Angeles Herald that the lassoing was 'yesterday' and the lynching 'Last night'. The fuller wire, the Huntsville Gazette and the Ottawa Free Trader agree on June 26, and the name of the man lassoed also varies between Hutter, Hutten, Hatter and Hunter.

reader.title: Lynching of Navajo Frank
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A crowd of citizens forced the Las Vegas jail, took out a prisoner held for lassoing a man, and hanged him from a telegraph pole (A4, A8, A13).

A 'crowd' or 'party of citizens' took Navajo Frank by force from jail, where he was held for dragging R. H. Hutter with a lariat, and hanged him (A4, A8, A13); the killing was punishment for that alleged act. The victim is described as an Indian, not Black, so the case falls outside anti-Black scope.
The St. Louis wire (A4, A8), a separate June 29 Las Vegas dispatch (A11) and a variant account (A12) all report the jailing and lynching, though they differ on its timing.

accounts.label: Las Vegas dispatch of June 29

accounts.label: Ottawa Free Trader variant
accounts.gist: Lynched early Monday morning for lassoing 'R. H. Hunter'; adds that Frank had been in Billy the Kid's gang and had killed twenty men and several women.

framing.detail: Headlines 'A Fiendish Deed', 'Brutality Punished', 'A Noose for a Noose', 'Lynched by Indignant Citizens' and 'A FIEND'S FATE' presented the hanging as deserved punishment of 'the fiendish Indian'.
Most papers ran the St. Louis special without comment under neutral or crime-column heads ('AN INDIAN LYNCHED', 'CRIMINAL', 'LATE NEWS ITEMS').
The Ottawa Free Trader paired the case with a Raton lynching under 'Judge Lynch' and added an unsupported record of twenty killings.
